title: Latitude Longitude Validator: Range and Format
description: Validate a latitude/longitude pair with the Latitude Longitude Validator — range checks, swaps and format sanity in one pass. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the pair (104.2, 39.7) fails instantly — no latitude exceeds 90 — and the validator's swap suggestion (39.7, 104.2, Denver's hemisphere with a sign question) is the diagnosis most bad data needs.
quick_answer: The Latitude Longitude Validator checks a coordinate pair for range, format and the classic errors — latitudes beyond ±90, longitudes beyond ±180, swapped axes and implausible hemispheres. Paste the pair and read the verdict: valid, or invalid with the specific reason and the likely fix.

Building a form that accepts coordinates? The validator's check list is the specification your validation should implement.
Sample rows from a legacy file, validate, and let the failure pattern (all swapped? all unsigned?) diagnose the whole file.
(-122.4, 37.8) claims latitude −122.4 — impossible. Swapped, it is San Francisco. The validator proposes the swap because the swap is the world's most common coordinate error.

(40.758, 73.986) passes every range check — and sits in Kazakhstan, not New York. Validation proves form, not truth; hemisphere context is the second gate, and the validator flags the question rather than the verdict.

faq: Range (±90/±180), numeric form, likely axis swaps and — with context — hemisphere plausibility, reporting each failure specifically.
Can I rely on this for professional work?
The checks are deterministic and complete for form validity — rely on them. Truth of location remains a data-provenance question, as the 'valid but wrong' example shows.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — the frame GPS produces and web maps consume.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — resolution is not accuracy; the precision tools on this site price each decimal place in metres.
A latitude of 0.71 is legal — and is Times Square in radians. The validator can flag suspiciously small pairs when the context smells of radians.
Perfectly — and the most suspicious valid pair in existence (Null Island collects every defaulted dataset). The validator passes it and raises an eyebrow in the notes.
The validator does not punish decimals; the precision tools judge their honesty. Form first, philosophy second.
